recent_posts.title: copilot.el 0.4
recent_posts.summary: copilot.el 0.4 is released, marking a major milestone by migrating from a reverse-engineered API to the official GitHub Copilot Language Server LSP protocol. Key changes include proper LSP client behavior (textDocument notifications, workspace folders, clean shutdown), interactive AI model selection, a rewritten parentheses balancer using parse-partial-sexp for syntactic awareness, improved server communication (status reporting, progress tracking, request cancellation, UTF-16 position support), a new 120+ test suite using buttercup with CI across multiple Emacs versions and platforms, and a fully rewritten README. Notable bug fixes include removing the company-mode dependency and fixing Emacs 30 compatibility. Upcoming features in development include Next Edit Suggestions, Copilot Chat, and native installation without Node.js.

recent_posts.title: Flycheck 36
recent_posts.summary: Flycheck 36 is out, marking the biggest release since the current maintainer took over. Highlights include two new checkers (javascript-oxlint using the Rust-based oxlint linter, and org-lint for Org mode), a security fix for CVE-2024-53920 in the emacs-lisp checker to prevent arbitrary code execution during byte-compilation, and ShellCheck improvements with new configuration options. Quality-of-life updates include automatic re-checking after buffer revert, info-level errors in the mode-line, and better Pyright/Ruff integration. Over 25 bug fixes were included, along with removal of deprecated checkers (TSLint, Ruby Sass tools, Erubis, CSSLint, etc.). The documentation site flycheck.org received a visual refresh with the Furo theme. Looking ahead, Flycheck 37 plans include tree-sitter integration, OCaml and Swift checkers, and potentially dropping Emacs 27 support.

recent_posts.title: adoc-mode 0.8
recent_posts.summary: adoc-mode 0.8 is a major release of the Emacs major mode for AsciiDoc editing. Key new features include native syntax highlighting for code blocks using the appropriate language major mode, inline image previews (including remote images), improved navigation with adoc-follow-thing-at-point and hierarchical imenu, and highlighting of Asciidoctor-specific inline macros. The release also fixes numerous long-standing bugs including typing lag in code blocks and Emacs hangs from escaped curly braces. Internally, the minimum Emacs version is bumped to 28.1 and the codebase has been restructured. The author also announces asciidoc-mode, a separate lighter-weight tree-sitter-based alternative for Emacs 30.1+.

recent_posts.title: nREPL 1.4
recent_posts.summary: nREPL 1.4.0 introduces the ability to pre-configure default values for dynamic variables across all local nREPL servers, with the most practical use being enabling *warn-on-reflection* globally. The release also adds client identification features for session tracking and drops support for Clojure 1.7, marking only the second time runtime requirements have been updated in over 7 years.

recent_posts.title: Weird Ruby: Anonymous Heredocs
recent_posts.summary: Ruby developers proposed an anonymous heredoc syntax that would eliminate the need for delimiter names, using `<<~` and `~>>` instead of traditional named delimiters like `<<~MARKDOWN`. While this proposal was rejected, developers can achieve similar brevity by using a single underscore `_` as the delimiter name, creating cleaner-looking heredoc syntax for multi-line strings.

recent_posts.title: CIDER 1.18 ("Athens")
recent_posts.summary: CIDER 1.18, known as 'Athens', marks a significant release with numerous new features, enhanced efficiency, and improved maintainability. Key changes include dropping support for Boot and Emacs 26, reducing third-party dependencies, and optimizing error handling. Updates to the inspector and improvements in completion and dynamic font-locking further enhance the user experience. Despite these advancements, financial support for CIDER has notably decreased over the past three years.

recent_posts.title: State of CIDER 2024 Survey Results
recent_posts.summary: The 2024 State of CIDER Survey reveals a stable and mature user base, with most users having 5+ years of experience. Despite a drop in survey participation compared to 2019, CIDER remains popular among both professionals and hobbyists. Users generally keep up with the latest versions of CIDER and Emacs, and installation through package.el remains the most common method. Although documentation is rated highly, there's room for improvement, especially in onboarding and advanced features. Donations for supporting CIDER have decreased since 2022, highlighting a need for continued community support.

recent_posts.title: Projectile Introduces Significant Caching Improvements
recent_posts.summary: Projectile has introduced significant caching improvements by creating individual cache files for each project, leading to faster loading times. The cache is now read from disk only when needed, and the initialization process has been optimized to avoid IO operations. Version 2.9 will include multiple bug fixes and is poised to offer enhanced functionality.

recent_posts.title: A Simpler Way to Deal with Java Sources in CIDER
recent_posts.summary: A new feature in the latest CIDER MELPA build allows users to effortlessly download Java sources for third-party libraries without using enrich-classpath. This functionality can be enabled by toggling the variable cider-download-java-sources. It works for both tools.deps and Leiningen-based projects, launching a subprocess for either clojure or lein binary. While this method is efficient, issues might occur with private dependencies. User feedback is needed to refine this feature, which is planned to be enabled by default in CIDER 1.18.

recent_posts.title: State of CIDER Survey (2024)
recent_posts.summary: The CIDER community is invited to participate in the 2024 'State of CIDER' survey to influence the future development of the tool. The survey aims to collect valuable data on feature usage and user preferences, which will help in shaping CIDER 2.0. Feedback on several important aspects like Emacs and Java support, and potential areas of improvement are also sought. The responses will play a crucial role in creating an accurate roadmap for future releases.
